title: David shouting at God
hook: David shouting at God — anger is allowed
carry: you can say anything to him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter. The women at the tomb at first light. Your line: the stone is already moved. Did you catch yourself worrying on the road? Day sixteen.

Think of the last time you were really angry. At a person. At your life. Maybe, if you're honest, at God, or the universe, or whoever runs things. Most people assume that's the one feeling you can't bring to church. You're supposed to show up polite. Now open the middle of the Bible, and you'll find a whole book of people who didn't. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" That's not a complaint about God. It's a complaint to God, out loud, and it's scripture. Today's word is that book.
screen: `THE LAST TIME YOU WERE ANGRY.` → `YOU'RE SUPPOSED TO BE POLITE.` → `"HOW LONG?"`

segments.voice: The Psalms. A hundred and fifty poems, the songbook of ancient Israel, still prayed every day by Jews and Christians alike. The name comes from Greek, psalmos, a song sung to a plucked string instrument. The Hebrew title is Tehillim: praises. Tradition ties many of them to David, the shepherd boy who became king. The headings put his name on about half of them; scholars debate how many he actually wrote. Here's the surprise. For a book called praises, a great deal of it is complaint. Scholars call these laments, and by many counts they're the most common kind of psalm in the book. Psalm 13 opens: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" It asks how long four times. Psalm 22 begins with the line from the cross you heard two days ago: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" And Psalm 88 ends in darkness, with no comfort at all. It just stops. These weren't hidden away. They were sung, in public, together. Most laments have a shape. First the honest part: where are you, this isn't fair, I'm going under. Then, often, a turn. Psalm 13, after all its how longs, ends by saying the singer has trusted in God's mercy and will sing again. The anger doesn't have to be cleaned up first. It's the way in. That's why monks, soldiers, prisoners and people in hospital beds have prayed the Psalms for centuries upon centuries. There's a psalm for almost every feeling, including the ones people think they aren't allowed to have.
screen: `TEHILLIM — PRAISES.` · `MOSTLY? COMPLAINT.` · `"HOW LONG?" FOUR TIMES.` · `FIRST THE HONEST PART. THEN A TURN.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T HAVE TO BE POLITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe. Now think of something you're upset about. Not a crisis, but something real. Something you've been keeping polite about. And, silently, say it straight. No softening. How long. Why. This isn't fair. If you pray, you can say it to God, the way the Psalms do. If you don't, say it to the quiet. Then just breathe, and notice what's left once it's been said. You don't have to fix anything. The bell holds the time.
The Psalms. A hundred and fifty songs, with praise and complaint side by side. Sixteenth word.
Your line: you can say anything to him. Today, say one true thing you've been keeping polite. In a prayer, in a journal, or to someone safe. Day sixteen.

howItsDone: Christians sing and pray the Psalms in almost every kind of service, and many read one every day. In monasteries and in the daily prayer of many churches, the Psalms are prayed in order, all 150, over a set cycle.

options: only the praise. keep the complaint private.

original.note: Hebrew. praises — the book's own name, even though so much of it is complaint.

trapdoor: what you thought: calm, pious poems for quiet moments.
what it means: a songbook with room for every feeling — praise, grief, even anger at God.
what a scholar hears: by many counts laments are the largest group, and the Greek psalmos first meant a song sung to a plucked string.
